meta.titre: Raising Agents in Baking: Gases, Types and the Work of Yeast
meta.sous_theme: Mechanical, chemical, biological and steam raising agents

source.epreuve_titre: GCE O/L Food and Nutrition past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: On a market morning in Bamenda, a baker's dough is left in a warm corner and swells to double its size, while a cook next door whisks eggs until they are thick and pale before making a cake. Both cooks are doing the same job: putting gas into a mixture so that it becomes light. Raising agents are tested every year at the GCE, sometimes as a list of exact points and sometimes as an explanation of a process.

items: Flour contains protein that forms gluten when mixed with water.
A gas takes up more space when it is heated.
Yeast is a living organism that needs food, moisture and warmth.

sections.titre: Raising agents: gases, types and how each one works
sections.contenu_markdown:
### What a raising agent does
A raising agent puts gas into a mixture. In the heat of the oven the gas expands and the mixture rises and becomes light and porous. Only three gases are used: **air**, **carbon dioxide** and **steam**. The proteins of flour (gluten) and of egg stretch round the gas bubbles and then set (coagulate) in the heat, which fixes the open texture.

### Types of raising agent
| Type | How it works | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanical (physical) | air is trapped by the work of the cook | sieving flour, creaming fat and sugar, whisking eggs, beating, rubbing in, folding in, rolling and folding pastry |
| Chemical | a chemical reaction releases carbon dioxide | baking powder, bicarbonate of soda, self-raising flour |
| Biological | living yeast makes carbon dioxide | yeast in bread and buns |
| Steam | water in the mixture becomes steam in a hot oven | choux pastry, pancakes and batters |

### Chemical raising agents
Baking powder is a mixture of bicarbonate of soda (sodium hydrogencarbonate), a dry acid such as cream of tartar, and a starch filler that keeps the powder dry. It gives off carbon dioxide when it is moistened and heated. Bicarbonate of soda used alone also gives off carbon dioxide when heated. Self-raising flour is plain flour with baking powder already mixed in. Too much raising agent gives a coarse texture and a soapy or bitter taste, and the product may rise and then fall; too little gives a heavy product.

### Yeast and fermentation
Yeast is a tiny living fungus. It needs food (sugar), moisture and warmth. Its enzymes break the sugar down into **carbon dioxide and alcohol**: this is **fermentation**. The gas is trapped by the stretched gluten, so the dough swells during proving. In the oven the dough first rises further, then the heat kills the yeast and sets the gluten, and the alcohol evaporates. Cold slows yeast, and too much heat kills it.

variantes.quand_utiliser: For "list", "name" or "state" questions asking for a stated number of raising agents or gases.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Count your answers against the number asked and write each one as a short separate line. Name each agent exactly: for mechanical agents write sieving, creaming, whisking, beating, rubbing in or folding. If the mark is for the type, say whether it is mechanical, chemical or biological. For gases the full list is air, carbon dioxide and steam.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to explain how yeast raises a dough.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Give the steps in order: yeast is mixed with sugar, warm liquid and flour; it feeds on the sugar by its enzymes; carbon dioxide and alcohol are produced; the gas is trapped in the gluten and the dough rises; baking kills the yeast and sets the structure. Name the conditions needed: food, moisture and warmth.

variantes.nom: Choosing the agent for a product
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked which raising agent suits a given food and why.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Bread and buns: yeast, because the dough is strong with gluten and has time to ferment. Sponges: air from whisking or creaming. Scones and many cakes: baking powder or self-raising flour, because they work quickly. Choux pastry: steam, because the mixture contains a lot of water and eggs.

sections.enonce_markdown: Name three mechanical methods of putting air into a cake mixture, and explain why the mixture rises and sets when it is baked. (6 marks)

etapes.action: Read the command words and the marks.
etapes.justification: "Name" needs short answers and "explain" needs reasons. Six marks suggest three marks for the methods and three for the explanation.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Part 1: three methods. Part 2: three reasons covering rising and setting.

etapes.action: Choose three methods and say what each does.
etapes.justification: A method named with its effect earns the mark more safely than a bare word.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Sieving the flour: air is trapped between the particles. Creaming fat and sugar: air is beaten into the fat as small bubbles. Whisking the eggs: the egg white stretches into a foam full of air.

etapes.justification: The reason must name what expands.
etapes.resultat_markdown: In the hot oven the trapped air expands and the water in the mixture turns to steam, which also expands, so the mixture rises.

etapes.justification: A cake keeps its shape only if its structure becomes firm.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The proteins of the flour and the egg coagulate in the heat, so they set round the gas holes and fix the light texture.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **Methods:** sieving the flour, creaming fat and sugar, and whisking the eggs, each traps air. **Rising and setting:** in the oven the air and steam expand and lift the mixture, and the proteins of flour and egg coagulate and set round the holes, so the cake stays light.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing "yeast, flour and sugar" when asked for the conditions that yeast needs.
items.pourquoi_faux: Flour is not a condition. Yeast needs food (sugar), moisture and warmth.
items.correction_markdown: Answer with food, moisture and warmth, and add that too much heat kills it.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that baking powder and yeast make the cake rise "by themselves" without naming the gas.
items.pourquoi_faux: The mark is for the gas. Baking powder and yeast both release carbon dioxide, which expands in the heat.
items.correction_markdown: Name carbon dioxide, and say that it is trapped in the mixture and expands on heating.

items.erreur_markdown: Listing "oven" or "heat" as a mechanical raising agent.
items.pourquoi_faux: A mechanical agent is a method that traps air by the work of the cook. Heat only makes the gas expand.
items.correction_markdown: Write sieving, creaming, whisking, beating, rubbing in or folding.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that yeast makes dough rise by producing oxygen.
items.pourquoi_faux: Fermentation gives carbon dioxide and alcohol, not oxygen.
items.correction_markdown: Write that yeast ferments sugar into carbon dioxide and alcohol.

items.erreur_markdown: Adding extra baking powder to be sure that the cake will rise well.
items.pourquoi_faux: Too much gives a coarse texture and a soapy taste, and the cake may sink after rising.
items.correction_markdown: Measure the raising agent exactly as the recipe says.

items.enonce_markdown: (a) Name the three gases used to raise baked mixtures. (b) State the type of raising agent (mechanical, chemical or biological) in each case: whisking egg whites, adding baking powder, using yeast in dough.
items.solution_markdown: (a) **Air, carbon dioxide and steam.** (b) Whisking egg whites: **mechanical**. Baking powder: **chemical**. Yeast: **biological**.

items.enonce_markdown: A recipe for 12 buns uses 300 g of flour and 6 g of dried yeast (assumed values). A baker wants to make 30 buns. (a) Find the mass of flour and of yeast needed. (b) Flour costs 700 FCFA per kilogram and the yeast costs 8 FCFA per gram. Find the total cost of these two ingredients and the cost per bun.
items.solution_markdown: (a) Multiplying factor: $30 \div 12 = 2.5$. Flour: $300 \times 2.5 = 750$ g, so **750 g**. Yeast: $6 \times 2.5 = 15$ g, so **15 g**. (b) Flour: $0.75 \times 700 = 525$, so $525$ FCFA. Yeast: $15 \times 8 = 120$, so $120$ FCFA. Total: $525 + 120 = 645$, so **$645$ FCFA**. Cost per bun: $645 \div 30 = 21.5$, so **21.5 FCFA** per bun.

items.enonce_markdown: A cook mixed dried yeast into very hot water, added sugar and flour, and left the dough in a cold room for one hour. The dough did not rise. (a) Give three reasons why it failed. (b) Explain how the cook should have prepared the dough. (c) A scone recipe needs 5 g of baking powder for every 200 g of flour. How much baking powder is needed for 500 g of flour?
items.solution_markdown: (a) The very hot water killed the yeast. The cold room slowed the little yeast that was alive, so little carbon dioxide was made. One hour was too short for the dough to rise in the cold. (b) Mix the yeast with warm (not hot) liquid and a little sugar, add the flour, knead so that the gluten forms, and leave the dough covered in a warm place until it has doubled in size; then bake. (c) $500 \div 200 = 2.5$ and $2.5 \times 5 = 12.5$, so **12.5 g** of baking powder.

items_markdown: A raising agent puts gas into a mixture; the three gases are air, carbon dioxide and steam.
Mechanical agents trap air: sieving, creaming, whisking, beating, rubbing in, folding. Chemical agents: baking powder, bicarbonate of soda, self-raising flour. Biological agent: yeast.
Yeast needs food, moisture and warmth; fermentation turns sugar into carbon dioxide and alcohol; too much heat kills yeast.
Baking powder gives off carbon dioxide when moist and heated; too much gives a coarse texture and soapy taste.
In the oven the gases expand, then the proteins of flour and egg set the structure.
In list questions give exactly the number asked; in explain questions give the reason, not only the name.
